newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pro-Kashmiri militants hurl threats at India.
newsitem.headline: Pro-Kashmiri militants hurl threats at India.

text.p: The leader of Pakistan's Jamaat-i-Islami party said on Sunday there should be no compromise over the Kashmir dispute with India.
"Bilateral talks will not bear any fruit unless India recognises Kashmir as a disputed state," said the right-wing religious group's leader Qazi Hussain Ahmad.
He was addressing a rally of about 5,000 Pakistani supporters of a Kashmiri guerrilla group in Muzaffarabad, the capital of Pakistani-held Azad (Free) Kashmir.

Ahmad told the pro-Kashmiri militants banded into a Jamaat-i-Islami offshoot known as Al-Badr Mujahideen that if the government compromised on Kashmir, Pakistan's parliament and the president's house would turn into a "jail for rulers".
India and Pakistan, which have fought two of their three wars since independence in 1947 over Kashmir, resumed formal talks in March for the first time since early 1994.
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif is due to meet his Indian counterpart Inder Kumar Gujral on the sidelines of a regional summit conference in the Maldives next month.
Ahmad said the government should "give up the apologetic and cowardly attitude it has adopted" on Kashmir and give the militants material help.

Pakistan has long denied Indian charges that it arms, trains and finances separatist guerrillas fighting Indian rule in the two thirds of Kashmir under New Delhi's control. Islamabad says its support for the rebels is moral, political and diplomatic.
The rally was the climax of a two-day gathering of Al-Badr Mujahideen.

During a march earlier on Sunday, the militants shouted anti-Indian slogans. About a dozen paraded with Kalashnikov assault rifles and fired them in the air in defiance of a local ban on the display of weapons. Police took no action.
Bakhat Ameen, commander of Al-Badr Mujahideen, threatened to send his men across the ceasefire line to fight Indian troops unless New Delhi gave Kashmiris the right of self-determination.
Pakistan wants mainly Moslem Kashmiris to be allowed to vote whether to join Hindu-majority India or Islamic Pakistan. India says the Himalayan region is an integral part of its territory.
